The President of Finland and the Prime Minister of Norway have launched an international call for governance and control of development of frontier AI models. The call underscores that AI must be developed and used in line with international law. Chair, after years of progress, we are seeing backsliding of women's and girls' rights, sexual and reproductive health and rights, and gender equality. This is part of a broader pushback against human rights and inclusive participation. Institutions promoting gender equality are weakened. Funding is declining. Civic space is shrinking. Women in political and public life face more threats and violence, including coordinated online campaigns of sexist or misogynistic content. and direct or indirect threats of physical or sexual violence. I thank you, Mr. President. Let me join others in congratulating you and the members of your bureau On your election, we assure you of Eritrea's full support and cooperation during the committee's deliberations. Eritrea aligns itself with their statement delivered on behalf of the Group of 77 and China, and I wish to make the following statements in my national capacity. Mr. Chair, as we reflect on our collective commitments to human rights and social development, our deliberations must remain firmly anchored in the principles of the UN Charter, sovereign equality, political independence, noninterference in the internal affairs, and constructive international cooperation. The realization of full spectrum of human rights, including civil, political, economic, social, and cultural rights, as well as the right to development, requires genuine international solidarity, mutual respect, and an end to politicization, selectivity, and double standards. Human rights are universal, indivisible, interdependent, and interrelated. They must not be instrumentalized as political leverage, nor used as instruments of coercion against sovereign states. Yet regrettably, we continue to witness the pursuit of political objectives under the guise of human rights, including through punitive measures and intrusive country-specific mechanisms directed disproportionately at developing countries of the Global South. Such approaches undermine trust, deepen divisions, and divert attention from the genuine work of promoting and protecting human rights. Eritrea therefore reiterates its principled rejection of politically driven country-specific mandates and calls for a human rights architecture grounded in universality, impartiality, objectivity, dialogue, and cooperation and respect for national sovereignty. Mr. Chair, over the past 14 years, notwithstanding its non-recognition of the mandate, Eritrea has consistently participated in interactive dialogues with the Special Rapporteur on the situation of human rights in Eritrea and has responded to the issues raised. Yet the mandate has continued for more than a decade without providing a constructive framework for genuine cooperation. Its perpetuation has instead contributed to the recycling of politicized narratives concerning Eritrea. As Eritrea informed Member States during the 62nd regular session of the Human Rights Council, Eritrea has therefore decided that from this session onwards, it will no longer participate in the interactive dialogue with the Special Rapporteur in the Third Committee. This decision should not be misconstrued as disengagement from the international human rights system. Eritrea will continue to engage with the human rights treaty bodies, the Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights, and the Universal Periodic Review in accordance with its international obligations and commitments. Eritrea is also concerned by the increasing resort to block voting in the Human Rights Council, where political alignments can at times appear to precede objective consideration of the issues before the Council. A Council established to promote universality and objectivity and non-selectivity should not become an arena of political arithmetic. Eritrea has endured years of listening to statements by member states with no presence in Eritrea, repeating allegations and narratives apparently prepared elsewhere, rather than engaging with the realities of the country. The Council consists of 47 member states, elected by the wider membership of the United Nations. Once elected, members assume a responsibility that extends beyond particular regional groupings and political affiliations. As the membership of the Council is renewed this month, Eritrea urges those entrusted with this responsibility to exercise judicious independence and institutional restraint. They sit not merely as representatives of particular blocs, but as members of a Council acting on behalf of the wider UN membership. Voting should therefore be guided by the merits of the matter before the Council, not predetermined alignments. The same standards should be applied consistently to all member states. The credibility of the Council will ultimately depend not on how effectively blocks can marshal votes, but on how faithfully its members uphold the principles and purposes entrusted to them by the United Nations membership. Mr. Chair, for Eritrea, human rights are not abstract ideals or externally imposed directives. They are rooted in human dignity, equality, and social justice, and are deeply embedded in our history and struggle for independence. Guided by self-reliance, social justice, and national ownership, Eritrea's development strategy seeks to create opportunities, improve livelihoods, and enable citizens to participate in, contribute to, and benefit from national development. Let me highlight four areas. First, gender equality and health. Gender equality remains an integral part of Eritrea's development. Legislative and institutional frameworks concerning labor, nationality, citizenship, and land have been strengthened to advance equal rights and opportunities. Eritrea has also maintained a comprehensive legal framework prohibiting and criminalizing female genital mutilation, complemented by sustained community-based efforts to promote its abandonment. In health, Eritrea has recorded important gains in reducing child and maternal mortality, expanding maternal and child health services and skilled birth attendance, and sustaining high childhood immunization coverage. Public health interventions have also contributed to a substantial reduction in malaria-related mortality. The strengthening of health information systems, disease surveillance, and national genomic sequencing capacity is further enhancing Eritrea's ability to detect and respond to health threats and to make evidence-based decisions. On education, Eritrea Education remains a central pillar to Eritrea's human capital development. Investment in educational infrastructure has expanded access to schooling, including to rural and underserved communities, while the expansion of early childhood education has created greater opportunities for foundational learning. Eritrea continues to invest in teachers, learning materials, monitoring systems, and educational infrastructure with particular attention to improving quality, equity, and participation by girls and women. Social protection, social justice has been a core principle since the liberation struggle. Eritrea has continued to expand social welfare programs and community-based support mechanisms, particularly for vulnerable and disadvantaged communities. Guided by the National Social Protection Policy and Strategic Plan, the government has substantially expanded social protection coverage with more than 90% of expenditure financed domestically. Programs support orphans and the vulnerable children, persons with disabilities, older persons, persons living with HIV and martyrs' families. Community-based rehabilitation now reaches the vast majority of the country, providing access to healthcare, rehabilitation, inclusive education, and assisted technologies. On agriculture and resilience, recognizing the vulnerability of agriculture to climate variability and recurrent drought, Eritrea has prioritized climate-smart agriculture, integrated water resource management, afforestation, watershed rehabilitation, and soil and water conservation. Over the past decade, the government has implemented a major water and soil conservation program, including the construction of more than 800 dams of various sizes, substantially enhancing national water storage and distribution capacity. The five-year strategic plan for 2024 to 2028 seeks to further transform agriculture into a more productive, sustainable, and climate-resilient driver of national development. Initiatives such as the minimum integrated household agricultural package and small and productive farm plot models are contributing to household food security and greater resilience in rural communities. Mr. Chair, despite limited resources and a challenging external environment, Eritrea continues to invest in the well-being and livelihood of its citizens. Such national efforts, however, can be significantly constrained when the international environment limits a country's access to the resources and opportunities necessary for development. Unilateral coercive measures can impede access to finance, development cooperation, essential goods and services, and the implementation of national development priorities. Eritrea therefore reiterates its call for the immediate and unconditional lifting of such measures. In conclusion, Mr. Chair, Eritrea reaffirms its commitment to constructive engagement, genuine dialogue, and the universal promotion and protection of human rights. Such engagement, however, can be meaningful when grounded in sovereign equality, political independence, non-interference in internal affairs, and mutual respect. Human dignity, social justice, and development are inseparable. The realization of human rights requires not only dialogue and international cooperation, but also an enabling international environment in which nations and peoples are able to determine their own priorities and translate them into tangible improvements in the lives of their citizens. Eritrea will continue to engage constructively with the international human rights system through the mechanisms and processes it recognizes. I thank you, Mr. Chair.

Madam Vice-Chair, distinguished delegates, colleagues, 77 years ago, having witnessed the devastation of the Second World War, states came together and adopted the Geneva Conventions. Today, we see that respect for these rules is eroding. In over 130 armed conflicts, The consequences fall hardest on those already most at risk. Sexual violence remains a pervasive feature of armed conflict. Thousands of people go missing, leaving families without answers. Children are recruited, increasingly through online means, and used to participate in hostilities, while attacks on schools deprive them of safe access to education. Persons with disabilities face barriers and heightened risks. Conflict is driving food insecurity to alarming levels. And medical personnel continue to be attacked, threatened, detained, or killed while carrying out the very duties that international humanitarian law, or IHL, protects. As the Third Committee begins its work during this 81st session of the General Assembly, the ICRC wishes to provide the following regarding agenda items now before the Committee. First, In 2025 alone, sexual violence perpetrated by armed actors was publicly reported in more than 30 conflict-affected countries, affecting millions of women, men, boys, and girls, including persons deprived of their liberty. In more remote frontline areas, where the ICRC is often one of the only few actors left, it's not uncommon for our teams to be approached by more than 50 victim survivors in one day. Risks of sexual violence are rising, in large part due to the expansion and fragmentation of armed conflict, the proliferation of small arms and light weapons, trust and training gaps among armed actors, and the growing use of information and communications technologies, or ICT, by weapon bearers to facilitate or perpetrate acts of sexual violence. Recent funding decreases across the humanitarian sector have also further compounded the consequences of sexual violence, with numerous frontline service providers forced to suspend their activities from one day to the next. This has left many victim survivors both with few options to safely seek help and at further risk of additional violence, reprisals, or needing to rely on unsafe coping mechanisms. The ICRC works to prevent, mitigate, and respond to sexual violence during armed conflict and other situations of violence. by engaging directly with weapon bearers on the front lines, including by reducing stigma through community outreach, together with its Red Cross Red Crescent movement partners. The number of people going missing in today's conflicts is unacceptably high. Too many families are being left in the agony of not knowing the fate of their loved ones and are often not supported. This is not inevitable. So much more can be done to prevent people from going missing. IHL obliges all parties to armed conflicts to prevent disappearances, to search for, collect and evacuate the dead without distinction, to account for the missing, and to share any information with families. In situations of international armed conflict, states parties to the Geneva Conventions must establish national information bureaus to account for protected persons in their hands and transmit this information through the ICRC's Central Tracing Agency. This has an important protective function. Parties must treat the deceased with dignity, must identify, and where possible, must return mortal remains to families. Concrete suggestions in this regard are offered in the recently published outcome documents of the Global ICL Initiative, as well as in a recent ICRC report on how non-state armed groups can prevent people from going missing. The digitalization of armed conflict is transforming the ways in which children can be recruited, and used in hostilities. Physical proximity to armed actors is no longer always necessary. Through social media, messaging applications, and online gaming platforms, children are recruited or tasked remotely. Given their age and evolving capacities, children are particularly vulnerable to manipulation. Digital technologies may offer new pathways into armed conflict, but the resulting harm to children is no less real. The law is clear. The prohibition against the recruitment and use of children in hostilities does not stop at the digital frontier. All states have obligations to take measures to prevent the recruitment and use of children in hostilities, including when related acts are facilitated by ICT. The Global IHL Initiative's Workstream 6 outcome document sets out recommendations as to how governments can improve compliance with these rules in the online sphere. The principle underpinning these efforts is simple: children must be protected from being drawn into the fight online as well as offline. In armed conflicts today, millions of children are denied safe access to education, a trend that continues to rise at alarming rates. Disruptions to education can entrench cycles of poverty, weaken social cohesion, and increase the risk of future conflict. The protection of education during armed conflict is firmly established in IHL and international human rights law. We encourage States to develop doctrine and codes of conduct to avoid, to the maximum extent feasible, the use of educational facilities for military purposes. Persons with disabilities face specific barriers and risks in armed conflict, from inaccessible warnings, shelters, evacuations and humanitarian assistance, to the risk of being attacked because they are erroneously perceived as a military threat. The Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities, or CRPD, which was adopted 20 years ago, specifically requires in its Article 11 that states parties protect persons with disabilities in armed conflict in line with their obligations under IHL and international human rights law. For the ICRC, this complementarity between IHL and the CRPD means taking the specific barriers and risks faced by persons with disabilities into account not only in humanitarian responses but also in military policies, training, planning, and conduct. With Switzerland, we organized a state expert meeting on IHL precautions this year, which also encouraged states to share their good practices in implementing disability-inclusive precautions, the results of which will be shared publicly shortly. Hunger in armed conflict is often the cumulative consequence of actions taken over time. Insecurity prevents farmers from reaching their fields. Markets are disrupted. Water and electricity systems deteriorate, affecting production and storage. Even disruptions to digital connectivity can deepen food insecurity, impacting supply chains and payment systems. In short, food systems depend upon interconnected infrastructure and services. Damage and disruption across these systems affect food availability and access far beyond the immediate area of hostilities. We cannot count on humanitarian relief alone to mitigate these impacts. Parties must comply with the absolute prohibition of starvation of civilians as a method of warfare. They must also respect and protect civilians and civilian objects and uphold the special protection of objects indispensable to the survival of the civilian population. In armed conflict, medical personnel enjoy specific protection under IHL. They must be respected and protected in all circumstances. Yet they're too frequently harmed, threatened, detained, or killed while performing duties the law explicitly safeguards. A wounded person's right to medical care and a doctor's duty to treat them, whether friend or foe, must be recognized, always and everywhere. Inseparable from the life-saving functions of medical personnel are also those of medical facilities. They, too, must be respected and protected under IHL to safeguard access by patients to care and to maintain health systems during armed conflict. However, today, we see a deeply troubling pattern of attacks, misuse, and impediments to the functioning of medical facilities. The outcome document of work stream 5 of the Global IHL Initiative underlines the specific protection of medical facilities under IHL and proposes practical measures based on state practice. Protecting civilians means upholding the promises states made when they acceded to the 1949 Geneva Conventions. The Global IHL Initiative provides every state with an opportunity to send a powerful signal that wars must have limits. We call on all states to make IHL a political priority, including by joining the initiative. And we encourage the highest level of participation on December 7th in Jordan at the Humanity in War conference. I thank you very much, Madam Vice-Chair.

In Nepal, discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity is punishable. Furthermore, Nepal recognized that the valuable contributions of civil society, human rights defenders, media and human rights institutions. Madam Chair, Nepal's experience demonstrates that constitutional guarantees, affirmative action, social investment and inclusive policies can translate national commitments into meaningful progress for people. in health and well-being, life expectancy has reached approximately 72 years. Maternal mortality has declined considerably. Child mortality has declined to 23 per 1,000 live births, undernourishment to 5.4%, and stunting among children under five to 24.8%. Women's leadership, their participation in decision-making and governance continues to grow. Women's representation in the Parliament has reached to historic 34.9%. Similarly, women constitute almost 42% of the elected representative in local government bodies. We continue to prioritize quality education, skill development, productive employment, innovations, and entrepreneurship for our youth. Following the Gen. Z movement last year and general elections this March, Nepal now has the youngest prime minister in its history, and youth representations in parliament has grown significantly. Our progress is further evident in strengthened representations, agency, and voice for every segment of the nations, alongside improved access to essential services and opportunities that enable to participate fully and meaningfully in national development. Madam Chair, while these achievements are encouraging, we recognize that gaps and challenges remain. Social development and human rights are inseparable. As the least developed, landlocked, and mountainous country, Nepal continues to confront persistent challenges related to poverty, employment, and structural vulnerabilities. Resource constraints, climate-induced disasters, economic shocks, and external excesses have had profound impacts on communities, particularly those already facing structural vulnerabilities. Disruption in energy and supply flows have driven up food and fuel prices, limited employment opportunities, reduced remittances, and increased global market volatility. These pressures have disproportionately affected women, children, persons with disabilities, indigenous people, Dalits, migrant workers, and those living in remote mountain and rural areas, deepening inequalities and slowing recovery. AI and digitalization have created new opportunities for innovation and inclusion, but they have also introduced risks such as digital harassment, discrimination, misinformation, and widening digital divide. Strengthening international cooperation, mobilizing resources, sharing technology and knowledge, and supporting inclusive policies and institutions are fundamental to building inclusive, peaceful, stable, and resilient society. On this, we must deliver on the international commitments, including the Sabiha commitment and the Doha political declaration. Mobilizing financial resources, expanding access to technology, and supporting capacity building at scale are essential to advancing sustainable and strengthening the resilience of communities around the world. We must also invest in the potential of young people by providing them with quality education and skill, decent employment opportunities, and meaningful participation in decision-making process. In conclusion, Madam Chair, we must place human dignity, inclusion, resilience, and human agency at the heart of our collective endeavor. Nepal remains committed to to working constructively with member states, the United Nations systems, human rights mechanisms, civil society, women, youth, local communities and other stakeholders to deliver on our collective global commitments and frameworks. Through stronger global solidarity and renewed multilateralism, let us build a sustainable future where development leaves no one behind. Technology serves humanity, and every person can live with dignity, equality, security, and hope. I thank you.

I thank the Permanent Representative of Nepal. We have heard the last speaker on my list for this meeting. Much, Madam Vice Chair. I regret that Germany, Sweden, Iceland, the United Kingdom, the European Union, Australia, Estonia, Lithuania, and the Israeli regime have once again used this hall to question Iran and to absolve themselves. Iran rejects these unfounded accusations in full. Peaceful assembly is protected. Organized violence, sabotage, and foreign-directed riots are not. To recast the restoration of public order as crimes against humanity is a political act, not a legal one. Nobody is killed for holding an opinion. Courts do not execute dissidents. The death penalty is only imposed for the most serious crimes under Iranian law. The charge of systematic repression are equally false. Women in Iran vote, study, work, legislate, and practice their professions. Recognized ethnic and religious minorities have their worship, their languages, and their representation. The Israeli regime has the least standing of all. A regime of prolonged occupation, responsible for the killing of tens of thousands of Palestinians, cannot complain of the consequences of its own wars. Its account of missiles and shelters omits the aggression against Iran. Those who arm that regime, Germany and the United States foremost, and those who shelter it in every vote, do not acquire the right to lecture Iran and others on human rights. The European Union's list is the method let bear. Adversaries named, allies footnoted, and selectivity called principle. The United Kingdom, Australia, Sweden, Iceland, Slovenia, Lithuania repeat the same brief as if repetition were evidence. Selective outrage is not international law. Iran will not take instruction on human rights from those who bomb, occupy, or look away. Thank you.
Now I give the floor to the distinguished representative of India.

I give the floor to the representative of Serbia.

Thank you.
I give the floor to the representative of Israel.

Thank you, Madam Chair. I am taking the floor in exercise of my right of reply in response to the inflammatory and unfounded delegations made earlier by Iran. I will also use this opportunity to address some of the comments we have heard from certain delegations against my country over the past two days. Let me begin with Iran. A regime that has for decades financed, armed, trained, and fueled terrorist organizations across the Middle East and beyond has little credibility when it speaks about human rights and international security. Iran supports Hamas, Hezbollah, the Houthis, and other armed terror groups. The Iranian regime have also been involved in supporting terrorist activities across Africa, Asia, Europe, and the Americas. Today, three years later, Hamas and other Palestinian armed groups still have not disarmed. And yet, in statements here, we repeatedly hear demands directed at Israel, with barely a word about the organization that launched this war, continues to maintain its military capabilities and continues to operate among Gaza's civilian population. We should also not ignore Hamas' exploitation of civilian infrastructure and the use of civilians, including children, in support of its military activities. Madam Chair, let me end on a positive note as we prepare for Shabbat. There is one point in which I believe we can agree, and was mentioned here by many member states. The people of our region, Israelis, Palestinians, and Iranians alike, deserve to live free from terror and violence and to build lives grounded in peace, stability, dignity, and opportunity. I thank you.
I give the floor to the representative of Ukraine.

Thank you, Madam Vice Chair. And the International Criminal Court has issued a warrant against Putin and his commissioner for children's rights for precisely this crime. Children are taken from their families, given Russian citizenships, placed with Russian families, and subjected to re-education. Thank you.
I give the floor to the representative of Democratic People's Republic of Korea.

Japan should honestly and truly apologize for its past war crimes before they seek for the permanent seat of the UN Security Council. Thank you, Madam Chair.
I give the floor to the representative of Greece.

Thank you, Chair. Greece is exercising the right of reply in response to baseless allegations regarding the Muslim minority in Thrace. The Muslim minority in Thrace consists of three distinct groups whose members are of Turkish, Pomak, and Roma origin. Each of these groups has its own spoken language and cultural traditions. Their common denominator is their Muslim faith. This is why the minority has been designated in the Lausanne Treaty of 1923 and is recognized by the Greek state as a religious one. Greece fully respects the principle of individual self-identification, but cannot accept attempts to assign to the religious minority a collective ethnic identity which is not their own. Persons belonging to the Muslim minority in Thrace fully participate in public, civic, and political life, including at the level of Parliament and as representatives in local authorities. There is also a special quota in civil service exams as well as in university admissions. Freedom of association is protected with numerous active associations. Greece is also engaging constructively with the Council of Europe to implement European Court judgments concerning associations in Thrace. On the other hand, The Greek Orthodox minority in Turkey has endured a long and painful history. Pogroms in 1955 and mass expulsions in the 1960s forced thousands from their homes. While the situation improved significantly over the decades, with fewer overt acts of violence, Long-pursued state practices of confiscations of properties, heavy taxation on assets, restrictions on access to certain professions, or using the Greek language have led to a dramatic shrinkage of the Greek Orthodox minority in Turkey. Following arbitrary confiscations, immovable properties belonging to Greek foundations have diminished from 8,000 in 1936 to approximately 500 properties today. Inheritance rights of Greek citizens of Turkish origin are curtailed, and minority schools survive only on private contributions, despite Lausanne guarantees. In view of the above, Greece would like to reiterate its commitment to fully protecting and respecting minority rights and calls on all UN member states to do the same. I thank you.

Jammu and Kashmir never was, neither is, nor will ever be, a so-called inalienable part of India. The world needs no lectures from such a serial violator of international law and a gross abuser of human rights. In Pakistan, a thriving democracy that embraces diversity and plurality, all our citizens, including minorities, enjoy all their constitutionally granted rights and freedoms. This is in stark contrast to the appalling situation in Indian state and society that has been consumed by Hindutva extremism, bigotry, hegemonic designs, and plain hubris. India's use of terrorism bogey and crying victim is fooling no one. India is a perpetrator of state terrorism in occupied Jammu and Kashmir. And India is a sponsor of terrorism that is taking the lives of Pakistani law enforcement personnel and citizens. India is actively aiding, abetting, and financing terrorist groups against Pakistan. Indian terrorism has even reached North American shores, Madam Chair. Pakistan remains firmly committed to dialogue, diplomacy, and peaceful settlement of disputes in accordance with the principles enshrined in the Charter of the United Nations. India would be well advised to also follow that path in the interest of regional peace, security, and stability, and prosperity and well-being of over 1.5 billion humanity that resides in South Asia. I thank you.
I give the floor to the representative of Iran on a second intervention.

I give the floor to the representative of Japan.

Japan will continue such contributions as a responsible member state of the United Nations. I will briefly touch upon Japan's position on the abductions issues in response to the statement made by the representative of DPRK. Japan's policy on North Korea is seek to normalize its relationship with North Korea in accordance with the Japan-DPRK Pyongyang Declaration through its normalization, both Japan and the DPRK would mutually waive all their property and claims and those of their nationals that had arisen from causes occurring before August 15, 1945, decided that they would discuss the issue of property and claims during the normalization talks. Japan's intention remains to seek to normalize relations with North Korea in accordance with Japan's DPRK declaration. Yes. I give the floor to the representative of Turkey.

Madam Chair, I take the floor to exercise the right of reply in response to the statement made by the distinguished representative of Greece regarding the Turkish minority in Western Thrace and Greek Orthodox minority in Turkey. The assertion that the Turkish minority faces no discrimination is regrettably inconsistent with the restrictions it continues to encounter in exercising its fundamental rights and freedoms. These concerns require concrete actions by the Greek authorities. The restrictions faced by the Turkish minority in Western Thrace in violation of bilateral and international agreements, particularly in the context of fundamental minority and human rights, such as education, freedom of religion and worship, are unfortunately on the rise. The rights of the Turkish minority in Western Thrace are guaranteed under the Lausanne Peace Treaty. Nevertheless, Greece continues to deny the Turkish minority's ethnic identity and its right to freedom of association. Its persistent refusal to register minority associations bearing the word Turkish in their names, despite the relevant judgments of the European Court of Human Rights, remains a matter of serious concern. These binding judgments must be implemented fully and without further delay. Many constructive steps towards the Greek Orthodox minority have been taken in Turkey in recent years in coordination with our Greek Orthodox citizens. Turkey has opened schools in Gokceada for only four students in response to demands of its Greek Orthodox citizens. Whereas Greece continues to shut down minority schools in Western Thrace and restrictions on the Turkish minority's educational rights also persists. Such actions are incompatible with Greece's treaty obligations and cannot be reconciled with assurances of equal treatment. Freedom of religion is another area of continuing concern. We would like to once again draw the attention of the international community to the fact that Greece does not recognize the elected religious leaders of an official minority in its territory. Respect for religious freedom requires due regard for the choices of the community concerned. We would like Greece to address these long-standing concerns, fulfill its obligations under the Lausanne Peace Treaty, implement the relevant judgments of the European Court of Human Rights, and engage in genuine dialogue with the Turkish minority. Thank you.
I give the floor to the Democratic People's Republic of Korea on a second intervention.

Thank you, Madam Chair. My second exercise right of reply will go to the Japan delegates. Your deliberate and your government's deliberate refusal to recognize the official name of the Democratic People's Republic of Korea, a sovereign state fully recognized under the international law, is more than just a diplomatic insult. Japan should honestly respond to our good faith and fully apologize for its past war crimes, the crimes against humanity. Thank you.

Thank you, Madam President. It is unfortunate that I am compelled to exercise my right of reply in response to the statement by North Korea a second time. I will not repeat here what I said. Thank you, Madam President.
